{{Short description|American psychologist (1940–2022)}}

'''William H. Tucker''' (1940–2022), also known as '''Bill Tucker''', was an American psychologist. He was an Emeritus Professor of [[Psychology]] at [[Rutgers University]] and the author of several books critical of [[Scientific racism|race science]]. He retired from Rutgers in 2009.<ref name="Rutgers Today">{{cite web |url= https://news.rutgers.edu/feature-focus/retiring-rutgers%E2%80%93camden-psychology-professor-stays-true-egalitarian-social-values-shaped-%E2%80%9960s/20091005|title= Retiring Rutgers–Camden Psychology Professor Stays True to Egalitarian Social Values Shaped by the '60s |last=Incollingo |first=Beth Fand |date=October 5, 2009 |website= |publisher=Rutgers Today |access-date= January 23, 2020|quote=}}</ref> Tucker died in 2022.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Winston |first1=Andrew S. |title=William H. Tucker (1940–2022). |journal=American Psychologist |date=January 2023 |volume=78 |issue=1 |pages=65–65 |doi=10.1037/amp0001071}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Tucker received his bachelor's degree from [[Bates College]] in 1967, and his master's and doctorate from [[Princeton University]]. He joined the faculty at Rutgers University in 1970 and was there since.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.bates.edu/news/1996/03/27/race-research/ |title=Psychologist to discuss the science of race research |date=1996-03-27 |website=Bates College |language=en |access-date=2018-01-12}}</ref> During his time as a student at Princeton, he was a member of the [[Students for a Democratic Society]] and participated in taking over buildings on campus.<ref name="Rutgers Today" />

==Career==
Tucker was a Psychometric Fellow for three years at Princeton, a position subsidized by [[Educational Testing Service]]. The majority of Tucker's scholarship was about [[psychometrics]], not in it. He sat on the advisory board of the [[Institute for the Study of Academic Racism]].<ref name="isar">[https://web.archive.org/web/20060207194059/http://www.ferris.edu/isar/avc.htm ISAR Advisor Council], Retrieved February 7, 2006</ref>

Tucker wrote critical commentaries on several [[hereditarian]] psychologists known for their controversial work on [[race and intelligence]]. He won the [[Anisfield-Wolf Book Award]] in 1995, and received a fellowship from the [[National Endowment for the Humanities]] in 2006.<ref name="Rutgers Today" />

According to his website, "My research interests concern the use—or more properly the misuse—of social science to support oppressive social policies, especially in the area of race.  I seek to explore how scientists in general, and psychologists in particular, have become involved with such issues and what effect their participation has produced."

== Publications ==
*Tucker WH (1994a). Fact and Fiction in the Discovery of Sir Cyril Burt's Flaws. ''Journal of the History of the Behavioral Sciences'', 30, 335–347.
*Tucker WH (1994b). ''[https://web.archive.org/web/20050830082054/http://www.press.uillinois.edu/s96/tucker.html The Science and Politics of Racial Research].'' University of Illinois Press. {{ISBN|0-252-02099-5}}
*Tucker WH (1997). Re-reconsidering Burt: Beyond a reasonable doubt. ''Journal of the History of the Behavioral Sciences'', 33, 145–162.
*Tucker WH (2002). ''[https://web.archive.org/web/20051221050148/http://www.press.uillinois.edu/epub/books/tucker/toc.html The Funding of Scientific Racism: Wickliffe Draper and the Pioneer Fund].'' University of Illinois Press. {{ISBN|0-252-02762-0}}
*Tucker WH (2005). ''The Intelligence Controversy: A Guide to the Debates.'' ABC-Clio, Inc. {{ISBN|1-85109-409-1}}
*Tucker WH (2009). ''The Cattell Controversy: Race, Science, and Ideology'', [[University of Illinois Press]]
*Tucker WH (2015). ''Princeton Radicals of the 1960s, Then and Now.'' MacFarland
*Tucker WH (2024). ''[https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-031-41614-9 'The Bell Curve' in Perspective: Race, Meritocracy, Inequality and Politics]'', Palgrave
